title: Selling volatility should support core positions, not replace them
summary: The speaker compares option income to taxes: a second-order effect. You would not sell a stock you like only for a tax loss. If selling volatility becomes the main return driver, you cap upside, add tail risk and lower long-run returns. Manage volatility around good core positions.

steps.caption: The bar is the whole portfolio. Each part has a different job.
Core: 80% in anchor positions you want to own. They drive most of the return.
Options overlay: about 10%. Selling volatility here complements the core.
Cash and reserves fill the rest and back any short options.
If option selling becomes the main driver, upside is capped and tail risk grows.
Main idea: treat option income like taxes, a second-order effect around the core.

takeaways: Option income is a second-order effect, like taxes.
Making short volatility the main return driver caps upside, increases tail risk and lowers total return over time.
Build good core positions first; use option overlays around them.
caveats: The 80/10/10 split is an illustration, not the speaker's number.
The transcript ends with a promotion for the speaker's website and waitlist.
